name: Quassia amara extract
lead: Quassia amara is a tropical shrub of the Simaroubaceae family whose extracts have been reported to have antiparasitic and anti-inflammatory properties.[1] A topical gel containing 4% quassia extract has been tested in small clinical studies in rosacea and facial seborrheic dermatitis.[1][2]
The evidence is limited to a 30-patient open-label rosacea study and a 60-patient randomized comparison in seborrheic dermatitis.[1][2] Other published work is in rats.[3][4]
No looksmaxxing-community material was found for this entry.

paras: The 4% gel has been investigated for rosacea of grades I to IV and for facial seborrheic dermatitis.[1][2]
A single-center, open-label study of 30 patients with rosacea grades I-IV examined the efficacy and safety of a 4% quassia extract gel.[1]
A randomized, double-blind study of 60 patients with facial seborrheic dermatitis compared the 4% gel with 2% ketoconazole and 1% ciclopirox olamine.[2]

In rats, a standardized extract reduced blood glucose in a diabetes model.[3] Another rat study reported that the extract and the compound 2-methoxycanthin-6-one, but not quassin, inhibited indomethacin-induced gastric ulceration.[4] These are not studies of skin or appearance.

card.summary: Herbal 4% gel tried in two small studies for rosacea and seborrheic dermatitis.
card.note: Evidence rests on one small open-label study and one small comparative trial.

quick.overview:
Quassia amara extract is a plant extract made into a 4% gel and tested in rosacea and facial seborrheic dermatitis.

The human evidence is two small studies, one of them open-label.
quick.mechanism: Researchers cite reported antiparasitic and anti-inflammatory properties of the plant.
quick.risks: Tolerability findings are in the original reports; no wider safety or regulatory data were found.
